title: Psalm 151

stories.title: 🎶 Psalm 151
summaryBullets: I was small among my brothers and the youngest in my father’s house; I tended my father’s sheep. (1:1).
My hands made a harp; my fingers fashioned a lyre. (1:2).
And who will tell my Lord? The Lord himself; it is he who hears. (1:3).
It was he who sent his messenger and took me from my father’s sheep and anointed me with his anointing oil. (1:4).
My brothers were handsome and tall, but the Lord was not pleased with them. (1:5).
I went out to meet the foreigner, and he cursed me by his idols. (1:6).
But I drew his own sword; I beheaded him and removed disgrace from the people of Israel. (1:7).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 16:11-13: Samuel anoints the youngest son from a horn of oil while he is keeping sheep.
1 Samuel 16:7: The Lord does not look on height or appearance but on the heart.
1 Samuel 16:23: David plays the lyre and Saul is relieved.
1 Samuel 17:43: The Philistine curses David by his gods.
1 Samuel 17:51: David takes the Philistine's own sword and cuts off his head.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἔξωθεν τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ (exothen tou arithmou, 'outside the number')
translationNotes.note: Greek manuscripts carry a heading before verse 1 that ascribes the psalm to David in his own hand, marks it as standing outside the number of the hundred and fifty psalms, and gives the occasion as his single combat with Goliath. A Hebrew form of the psalm was recovered among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּנּוֹר (kinnor) - Greek: ὄργανον (organon, 'instrument') and ψαλτήριον (psalterion)
translationNotes.note: Handmade stringed instruments, not concert harps. The kinnor was a small lyre, light enough for a shepherd to carry and play while walking with the flock. The psalm says his own hands made and fitted them.

translationNotes.term: Anointed me with his anointing oil
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה (shemen ha-mishhah) - Greek: ἔλαιον χρίσεως (elaion chriseos)
translationNotes.note: Olive oil poured over the head from a horn or flask. It was the legal act that installed a king or a priest, a public appointment rather than a blessing or a washing. 1 Samuel 16:13 records Samuel using a horn of oil on David in front of his brothers.

translationNotes.term: He cursed me by his idols
translationNotes.note: A curse sworn in a god's name was standard practice before single combat, an attempt to bind the opponent to a divine sentence before a blow was struck. 1 Samuel 17:43 records the Philistine cursing David by his gods.

stories.keyTakeaway: David recounts being youngest in his father's house, tending sheep, and making a harp and lyre by hand. The Lord sends his messenger, takes him from the flock, and anoints him, passing over his taller brothers. He meets the foreigner who curses him by his idols and beheads him with his own sword.

intro:
This psalm speaks in David's voice, and the Greek Psalter labels it as such. A superscription stands before verse 1: Houtos ho psalmos idiographos eis Dauid kai exothen tou arithmou, hote emonomachesen to Goliath (Οὗτος ὁ ψαλμὸς ἰδιόγραφος εἰς Δαυιδ καὶ ἔξωθεν τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ, ὅτε ἐμονομάχησεν τῷ Γολιαθ), meaning "This psalm is David's own writing and outside the number, when he fought Goliath in single combat." The phrase exothen tou arithmou, "outside the number," is why it carries no place among the hundred and fifty. It stands last in the Greek Psalter, after Psalm 150, in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (fourth century AD) and Codex Alexandrinus (fifth century AD).

The seven verses cover two episodes from David's youth. Verses 1-5 are the anointing: the youngest son in his father's house, keeping the sheep, making a harp and a lyre with his own hands, taken from the flock by the messenger God sent and anointed with the anointing oil while his taller and better-looking brothers stood by (1 Samuel 16:1-13; at 16:7 Yahuah tells Samuel that He does not look on height or appearance but on the heart). Verses 6-7 are the combat: the foreigner who curses him by his idols and loses his head to his own sword (1 Samuel 17:43, 51). The setting is Bethlehem and the Valley of Elah in the reign of Saul, in the years before David's own reign began at Hebron around 1010 BC.

A Hebrew form of the psalm was recovered at Qumran. The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, 11QPs-a (11Q5), found in February 1956 and copied in the first half of the first century AD, carries the material in its last column as two separate compositions, which its editor James A. Sanders labeled 151A and 151B. The first is headed "Hallelujah, by David the son of Jesse" and covers the ground of Greek verses 1-5 at greater length; the second is headed "At the beginning of David's power after the prophet of God anointed him" and breaks off shortly after taking up the Philistine. The Hebrew is longer than the Greek and its material is arranged differently: the Greek is a single psalm of seven verses that compresses the two Hebrew compositions, reorders part of what it keeps, and leaves the rest out.

The Orthodox churches receive it, and Greek and Slavonic Bibles print it after Psalm 150. The Armenian Bible carries it, and the Coptic Church reads it at the vigil of Bright Saturday. Some manuscripts of the Syriac Peshitta carry it together with four further psalms numbered 152 to 155. Jerome did not include it in the Vulgate, and the Council of Trent (1546) counted the Psalter at a hundred and fifty. It came into English late: William Whiston printed a translation in 1727, the 1611 King James Apocrypha does not contain it, and it entered English Bibles with the Revised Standard Version Expanded Edition of 1977.
